newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis shoot Palestinian at security check.
newsitem.headline: Israelis shoot Palestinian at security check.

text.p: Police shot and wounded a Palestinian near Tel Aviv on Thursday, saying he fled a security checkpoint set up to prevent anti-Israeli attacks to mark an Islamic leader's assassination.

When police at the Morasha junction discovered that the man, one of five Palestinian workers in a van, had forged identity papers, he fled for a field and refused their order to stop, they said. Police shot and seriously wounded him.
Israel was on high security alert ahead of the October 26 anniversary of the killing of Fathi Shqaqi, leader of the militant Islamic Jihad group behind suicide attacks in Israel.
Shqaqi was gunned down in Malta last year in what Palestinians believe was an attack by Israel's Mossad secret service. The militant group vowed to avenge his murder.

Israel set up roadblocks overnight to enforce a closure imposed overnight on the West Bank and Gaza Strip for fear of suicide attacks. Palestinians assail the closure as a collective punishment denying their workers jobs in the Jewish state.
Israel's Itim news agency said the wounded man, 25, was from Azoun village. The four other Palestinians were arrested.
It was unclear how they made it to the intersection in the heart of Israel, circumventing a West Bank closure. Police suspected they lacked entry permits to work in Israel.
Israelis also were remembering the assassination of prime minister Yitzhak Rabin on the first anniversary of his death according to the Jewish calendar.
The peace that was to be Rabin's legacy remained elusive as Israeli and Palestinian negotiators had yet to come to terms on a promised Israeli troop withdrawal from Hebron.
"There is still some progress but still the gap is wide...There are many problems," President Yasser Arafat told reporters in Palestinian-ruled Gaza City on Thursday.

Israel handed over other West Bank towns to Palestinian rule under a 1995 peace deal Rabin's government reached with Arafat. But it delayed the Hebron pullback after a spree of suicide bombings in February and March.

The election victory in May of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, long opposed to peace deals with the PLO, clouded the withdrawal from the city where 400 Jews militantly opposed to the pullback live and study among 100,000 Palestinians.

A religious Jew suspected of throwing hot tea at a dovish lawmaker in Hebron on Tuesday meanwhile turned himself into police, insisting he did not mean to pour it on her but that someone pushed his arm, spilling the tea in her face.
"I didn't pour it on her. For sure, I am sorry," Yisrael Lederman told reporters. "I offered her a cup of tea and someone pushed me."
Israeli media were quick to link the scalding tea that a Jew in a skullcap splashed in legislator Yael Dayan's face to the hollowed bullets another pumped into Rabin last November 4.
Dayan, daughter of the late Israeli general Moshe Dayan, was treated for burns to her face and chest.
